learningObjectives.text: How does he return and win?

betrayal.work: Fairy Tales From Far and Near
betrayal.author: Katherine Pyle
betrayal.locator: Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals; Pyle retelling · The Princes And The Friendly Animals, normalized characters 15869-17001
betrayal.excerpt: But after they had driven on and left the Prince lying there, the faithful animals did not desert him. They stayed beside him and mourned over him, and the lion licked his face and hands, but it could not revive him. Then the fox, which was very clever, reminded the animals of the flasks of ointment and healing water in the robbers’ house. The hare, which was very swift, said it would go and fetch the flasks, and it sped away to get them. Now the stepsister had wept the bowl full of tears of repentance and was free again; and when the hare came to the door and told her what it wanted, she gladly gave it the flasks and hung them about its neck in a little wicker basket. Then the hare fled back again to where the animals were waiting beside the Prince. With its tusks the boar broke the flask that held the ointment, and the bear rubbed it on the Prince’s wounds so that they were healed. Then they poured some drops from the second bottle between his lips, and the color came back to his cheeks and the light to his eyes. When they gave him to drink from the third bottle, he became quite well again and stronger than ever.
betrayal.note: Verbatim text from Katherine Pyle's 1922 English children's retelling. The collection labels it Lithuanian but does not identify an oral informant or underlying source text.

narrativeBlocks.title: The prize stolen
narrativeBlocks.body: The youngest prince wins the quest — the dragon beaten, the treasure or the bride taken — and on the way home, his own companions or brothers betray him: they take the prize and leave him for dead.

narrativeBlocks.title: Left in the pit
narrativeBlocks.body: He is thrown into a pit, or left wounded, or sent back in shame — the tale's darkest turn: the hero who did everything is robbed of the ending he earned.

narrativeBlocks.title: The healing herb's grace
narrativeBlocks.body: He survives — and in these tales a snake or a hare or a bird carries the healing that restores him: the wild's last debt repaid.

narrativeBlocks.title: The return that proves it
narrativeBlocks.body: He comes back — disguised or simply alive — and the truth comes out: the traitors are unmasked by his presence, and the reward he earned is finally his.

narrativeBlocks.title: Pyle's retelling
narrativeBlocks.body: This tale comes through Howard Pyle's Fairy Tales from the Far North — his own retelling of a Lithuanian story for American children: no informant, no source text, a literary adapter's voice. We hold it as retelling, not field-collection.

quiz.prompt: How is the youngest prince betrayed?

choices.text: His companions take the prize and leave him for dead — the earned victory stolen on the way home

quiz.explanation: The betrayal after the victory — the fairy-tale's darkest beat.

quiz.prompt: How does he win in the end?

choices.text: He is healed by an animal's grace and returns — his presence unmasks the traitors
He raises an army against them
He appeals to the dragon's spirit

quiz.explanation: The animal debts save him one more time — and the truth does the rest.
